content: 1. In settings where the prevalence of pretreatment HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) exceeds 10% (with a median of 19%), three strategies for addressing this issue were compared in terms of cost-effectiveness. Policy Option 1: Introduce a dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimen for all individuals initiating first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART). Policy Option 2: Implement pretreatment HIVDR testing for first-line ART initiators and switch those with detected NNRTI resistance to a DTG-based regimen. Policy Option 3: Take no action and continue using an NNRTI-containing regimen (e.g., tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] + lamivudine/emtricitabine [XTC] + efavirenz [EFV]) for all first-line ART initiators. 2. A model predicts that in sub-Saharan Africa, where the cost of a DTG-containing regimen is comparable to an EFV-based regimen, using DTG as the first-line treatment is cost-effective and may even result in cost savings. This is true regardless of the prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs at the country level, due to the benefits of DTG for individuals without drug-resistant HIV. 3. The cost-effectiveness of using a protease inhibitor/ritonavir (PI/r)-based regimen as first-line ART was not directly compared with DTG-based regimens in recent modeling studies. This is because PI/r regimens are more expensive in sub-Saharan Africa, and randomized trials have demonstrated the superiority of DTG as a first-line treatment for HIV. However, previous comparisons using the same HIV synthesis model showed that switching to a PI/r-based regimen was cost-effective when the prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs exceeded 15%, assuming a cost-effectiveness threshold greater than $2000 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. It is important to note that such a cost-effectiveness threshold is unlikely to be realistic in low-income settings. 4. Between February and March 2017, the World Health Organization (WHO) conducted an online survey of healthcare workers to assess challenges in transitioning from NNRTI-based first-line ART regimens to non-NNRTI-containing regimens. A total of 396 responses were received from healthcare workers in 61 countries, with 85% of respondents from lowand middle-income countries. The main challenges identified were the need for healthcare worker training and the lack of affordable and appropriately formulated alternative regimens. Notably, 42% of respondents reported starting all patients on the same NNRTI-based first-line ART regimen, regardless of perceived pretreatment HIVDR risk, while 25% reported using alternative regimens for individuals at higher risk of pretreatment HIVDR, such as those with prior NNRTI exposure. 5. A differentiated ART regimen approach, where non-NNRTI-based ART is used only for individuals at the highest risk of pretreatment HIVDR, was generally well-accepted. However, challenges included ensuring the availability of both standard and alternative regimens at clinics (66%), training healthcare workers (62%), and identifying eligible individuals (55%). 6. In a separate survey of ART program managers conducted by WHO in early 2017, 57 managers from 43 countries responded, with 82% from lowand middle-income countries. Of these, 77% found transitioning to a DTG-containing regimen for all new first-line ART initiators to be acceptable and feasible. The main challenges identified were cost (86%) and drug supply chain management (43%). 7. Among HIV experts surveyed at a WHO meeting in 2016, 81% indicated an urgent need to respond to pretreatment HIVDR. When presented with options, 37% favored switching all first-line ART initiators from EFV-based to DTG-based therapy, while 40% preferred introducing HIVDR testing to guide regimen selection. 8. In settings where individualized HIVDR testing is unavailable, introducing an alternative first-line regimen that includes DTG is likely to improve equity, even in countries with relatively low prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR. However, certain groups, such as pregnant women, individuals requiring concomitant treatment for tuberculosis (TB), and children, may not currently be eligible for standard DTG-based therapy due to limited safety and efficacy data. 9. Botswana and Brazil have implemented DTG-containing first-line regimens as part of their national policies. In Botswana, all newly initiating individuals were started on DTG-based ART as of June 2016, supported by a cost-effectiveness study. In Brazil, nationwide implementation of DTG for first-line ART began in January 2017, with an anticipated 82,000 individuals starting DTG-based therapy that year. The decision was driven by fewer adverse effects, improved viral suppression, and increasing NNRTI resistance. 10. The WHO Guideline Development Group reviewed evidence on pretreatment HIVDR testing to guide first-line ART selection. Due to a lack of direct evidence and concerns about feasibility and resource requirements, the group did not formally recommend for or against the use of pretreatment HIVDR testing for all individuals starting first-line ART. However, they acknowledged the potential individual benefits of such testing, particularly in high-income countries where it is standard practice.
